How my AI employees learn from their mistakes — the 4-write loop (and the rule nobody teaches) The exact loop that makes an AI actually learn from its mistakes — the one my AI employees run to come back sharper every week. Researchers proved it makes agents 14% better with zero retraining. Here's the whole thing: The idea: an AI is only as good as what's written in its files. So you build a loop that saves the RIGHT things, the right way. Four "writes": WHILE IT WORKS → the moment something durable shows up (a decision, a preference, a rule), it goes straight into the AI's memory file. The rule: if it won't change future behavior, don't save it. No diary of the day. THE SWEEP → a small, cheap model reads the conversation, pulls out what's worth keeping, checks it against the files, and updates them (update — don't pile on top). Run it right before a long chat gets compressed AND when it ends — that's exactly where details vanish. THE SLEEP PASS → once a night, a stronger model goes through the memory files like your brain does in sleep: merges duplicates, resolves contradictions (newest wins), turns ten messy notes into one clean rule. YOUR CORRECTIONS (the big one) → you don't fill out a form. You correct it in the chat like you'd correct a person — "never send that without asking me first." The sweep catches it and saves it with two things attached: WHY it was wrong + HOW to do it right next time. The rule that makes it stick: if the mistake was in HOW a task is done, put the fix in the SKILL — the instructions that get read every time the task runs — not in some memory diary it might never reopen. Guardrails so you don't poison it: every memory gets a date + a source, nothing's saved as "fact" until it's confirmed, money/identity stuff waits for your approval, and it all lives in plain files you can open and delete. The scoreboard: does it make the same mistake twice? That's the whole test. #aiagents #aiemployee #aiteam

THE LOOP → when it's wrong, you correct it like a person; the fix gets written back into the instructions, so it never makes that mistake twice. That's how it compounds — a little sharper every week. Your prompts are fine. You're feeding the AI nothing. Two people ask the same AI the exact same question. One gets a thin, generic answer. Everyone blames the same two suspects: the model ("I need the better AI") or the wording ("I need a better prompt"). Both are innocent. The AI answered blind. Here's the distinction that changes everything: Prompting is what you SAY. Context is what it HAS. Context means what's in front of the AI when it answers — your situation, your rules, your examples, your world. Person one gave it a question. Person two gave it a question sitting on top of three real things: the actual document, the rule that matters, one example of what good looks like. Same words. Different worlds. Pile two hundred things in front of the AI, and the one thing that mattered is buried — by you. The actual skill — the one almost nobody practices — works like an operating room. Before surgery, a nurse lays out ONE tray: the exact instruments this operation needs, in order. The supply closet stays down the hall. Before you ask your AI for anything, build its tray for THIS job: The two rules that apply One example of what done looks like The situation, in three sentences Picked fresh, every task. Your question can stay lazy — the tray does the heavy lifting. This is the line splitting everyone using AI right now. On one side: people polishing questions for a machine they keep in the dark — and it stays a party trick. On the other: people deciding what it has in front of it before it answers — and it does real work. Same model. Different skill. Context wins. And context is one piece of a whole set of skills like this — the set that puts you in the top one percent of people actually building with AI. Chat, automation, agent — the three words everyone mixes up If you've ever nodded when someone said "AI agent" and had no idea what they meant, this is for you. First: the confusion is the industry's fault. Everything gets called an agent now because "agent" sells. If these words have felt slippery, that's the words being misused — not you being slow. CHAT. You type a question, it types an answer, and then it WAITS. That last part is the whole definition. It'll sit there all day, perfectly capable, doing nothing, until you type again. Ask for a recipe, get a recipe — it will never shop for the ingredients and never wonder how dinner went. You move everything forward. Every time. AUTOMATION. Older than AI, and you've lived inside it for years. You sign up for something, a welcome email shows up — nobody typed that email. Somebody built it once, years ago, and it has greeted every person since. Something happens, so things happen: a trigger, then steps, in a fixed order, forever. The key: the thinking already happened. A person decided every step in advance. It's faithful, tireless and completely literal — and that's a FEATURE. For work that should happen identically every time, you want the literal one. AGENT. It has two things the others lack: a GOAL and a LOOP. You hand it an outcome instead of a step. It plans, does something, looks at the result, changes approach if that didn't work, and goes again until the goal is met. Ask it to plan a weekend trip within a budget: it searches, finds flights too expensive, tries different dates on its own, finds something that fits, checks the hotel is near the places you said you cared about, and comes back with a finished plan. Nobody told it to try different dates. It decided that mid-job, because the first attempt failed. SO HERE'S YOUR TEST — one question, works on every AI tool anyone will ever sell you: **Who decides the next step?** → You, every single time = CHAT → Decided in advance by whoever built it = AUTOMATION → The AI, while the work is happening = AGENT Chat waits for you. Automation follows the path. An agent chooses. That's it. You now understand the difference better than most people posting about it. And once you see the three clearly, the real picture shows up: they STACK. The best systems use all three — automations carrying the steady repeated work, AI dropped inside those automations for the judgment calls, agents taking whole jobs that need thinking through. Knowing which one a job actually needs is the skill. Reaching for an agent when a simple automation would do is the most expensive beginner mistake there is. Build an AI employee that answers your customer emails — in Claude Code, every step What it looks like working: overnight, 11 customer emails arrive. By the time you sit down, 9 have replies already written in your words, with the right prices and the right policy quoted. The other 2 sit at the top untouched and flagged — one person is angry, one wants money back, and those are yours. You read, you approve, you're done before your coffee cools. THE BUILD: 1 — THE DESK. Make a folder, open it in Claude Code, and write the job description in one line in CLAUDE.md: "you draft replies to customer emails for my review." One employee, one job. 2 — WHAT IT NEEDS TO KNOW. Plain files: what you sell and what it costs, your policies (shipping times, return window, what's covered), and the questions customers actually ask — which you know by heart. Help page or FAQ goes in too. This is what it pulls real answers from instead of inventing them. 3 — YOUR VOICE. The step people skip, then wonder why drafts sound like a robot in a call centre. Go to your sent folder, pull 20 replies you were happy with, paste them in a file. Twenty real examples teach your rhythm better than any instruction you could write. 4 — CONNECT THE INBOX, CAREFULLY. Grant READ. Grant DRAFT. Do NOT grant send. Delete stays off. A draft you don't like costs three seconds; a sent email you don't like costs a customer. 5 — WRITE THE PROCEDURE → SAVE IT AS A SKILL. Read the email, work out what it's about, find the answer in my files, write it in my voice, quote the real price or policy, and say which file it came from. Plus the instruction that matters most: if you can't find the answer in my files, SAY SO in the draft instead of guessing. Then: "save that procedure as a skill called customer-replies." 6 — THE ROUTING RULES (what makes it safe to leave running). Anyone who sounds angry → straight to you, no draft. Refunds and chargebacks → you. Anything legal → you. Anything it's unsure about → you. Everything else gets a draft. You're teaching it the difference between a question and a judgment call. 7 — TEST IT ON YOUR OWN HISTORY. Take 20 emails you already answered last month, run it on those, compare its draft to what you actually sent. You'll see exactly where it's wrong — an old price, a customer who'd already emailed twice, too formal. Every fix goes into the SKILL FILE, not into your head. Repeat until the drafts stop surprising you. 8 — LET IT RUN ON REAL MAIL. It drafts, you review. Your job becomes reading and approving instead of writing from scratch. Every correction from here follows the same rule: if it'll come up again, it goes in the skill. THEN, OVER WEEKS: as you watch it be right, you widen what it's allowed to do. The simplest category — the one it's been right about 40 times running — is the one you let send by itself. Money and angry customers stay gated behind your approval forever, because trust earned on easy questions doesn't transfer to hard ones. That's the build: one folder, its knowledge, your voice, a careful connection, a written procedure, hard routing rules, and a test against your own history. #aiemployee  #aiautomation #aiagent

# Three doors, one building: API, CLI, MCP API, CLI and MCP are three ways to connect an AI system to a tool. Picture one building with three entrances. 1. **API: the loading dock.** A program sends a precisely formatted request and receives structured data. Useful for bulk work, repeatable integrations and precise operations. Store private credentials in the connection settings, and test generated code. 2. **CLI: the staff entrance.** The command-line interface exposes commands a program or AI coding tool can run. When a CLI supports your task, the AI can read its help and use the documented commands within your account permissions. 3. **MCP: the front desk.** The server exposes a menu of tools an AI application can discover and call. Some connections use a simple sign-in; others need setup. Server and account permissions determine what is actually available. For a supported everyday task, start with a trusted MCP connection. Inside Claude Code, a supported CLI can be convenient. For scale or a custom integration, check whether the API exposes the operation you need. These routes can overlap: a CLI or MCP server often calls an API underneath. My Workspace employee reads email and fills sheets through the command line. Context engineering, explained simply · Brief your AI. Don't bury it. · The files behind an AI employee Context is the information an AI has available for the answer it is producing: your message, loaded instructions, relevant files, conversation history and tool results. Context engineering means choosing what belongs there and what should stay in the archive until needed. More information can make the job harder when it adds distractions. In Chroma's context research, focused extracts performed better than full conversation histories for the tested questions. That is a reason to organize and retrieve information carefully—not a claim that every longer prompt is worse. Here is how to put it into practice: 1. **Write the standing brief.** Use CLAUDE.md in Claude Code or AGENTS.md in Codex for concise project instructions: how you work, the important rules and where to look next. 2. **Build the library.** Keep offers, customers, processes and decisions in files. Give the agent a map and ask it to open what the current job needs. 3. **Package repeatable jobs as skills.** The agent can see a short description, then load the procedure when it selects that skill. 4. **Save useful corrections.** Check the note and make sure it is read when relevant. Storing a file alone does not guarantee the next answer will use it. 5. **Keep long jobs organized.** Compaction reduces the active conversation, but details can be lost. Keep important decisions in durable files and use focused helpers where the work benefits from them. Four habits: write outside the chat, brief without burying, load what the job needs with a map to the rest, and save the corrections that matter. #contextengineering #aiagents

What Jev actually is, why it's so fast, and what you can build with it. Classification is as old as AI that can read: give it text, ask a question with fixed answers (complaint yes/no · which team · urgency 1–5), and the label drives a rule. The problem: we've been using models built for writing, a few seconds per answer. Jev (TypeSafe, launched Sept 15, founded by one of the OpenAI researchers behind ChatGPT's instruction-following) only decides. It never writes. Send the text once with every question; it scores every answer in one pass: yes/no, pick one, or a score, each with a confidence. 70–500 ms. Input ~$0.042 per million tokens, output free. TypeSafe measured up to ~200× faster and ~400× cheaper than top models on its own workflows, and says real-world gains are usually lower. Builders: a resume screened against 6,000+ companies in 25 seconds for $0.37; 98,000 items labeled in ten minutes. ~13% of paid Vercel AI Gateway teams used it within a day. Calibrated: "70% sure" should be right ~70% of the time, so software can act alone above a threshold and route the rest to a person. Build with it: every competitor ad, same five questions · every ticket, review, call note and CRM entry across systems, tagged the same way · an agent's actions checked before they run (LangChain already does this). Edges: text only; weak at math, counting, dates; reads your question literally; you design the questions and categories up front. That design is the skill. #jev #aiagent

How a $50K AI project actually starts (process mapping, step by step) Before anyone builds anything, a real AI project starts with a stopwatch and a wall of sticky notes. Here's the whole method on one company: a 60-person parts distributor where 400 orders a day arrive as PDF attachments and six people retype them into the ERP. Interview the people who do the work, not the owner. The owner says taking an order is 5 steps. The person who's done it for nine years walks you through 41, including the sticky note on her monitor. Sit next to them with a stopwatch. Measure touch time (6 minutes of actual work) against lead time (3 hours from email to confirmation). The minutes cost wages. The hours cost customers. Break every box into atomic steps. One person, one system, one action. "Enter the order" is 11 steps. AI can't do "enter the order", but it's great at "match their part number to ours", and it tells you how sure it is. Hunt the exceptions. Old part numbers, price mismatches, backorders, credit holds, duplicate POs. Log them for two weeks. That's where the time goes. Give every step one of three colors. Blue is a rule, so automate it. Purple is judgment on messy input, so AI does it and a person approves when it's unsure. Orange is money or a relationship, so it stays human. Fix broken steps before you automate them. Score and sequence. Frequency × minutes × cost of a mistake gives you the roadmap. Track one number from day one: the share of orders nobody had to touch. Then the $50K has a shape: paid discovery, then phases that each pay for the next. Nobody loses their job. They stop retyping and handle the exceptions and the customers. #aiautomation #aiagent

How AI actually works (in plain English) How does AI actually work? It's guessing, one word at a time, and it's frighteningly good at it. AI like ChatGPT and Claude was trained on a huge pile of text: books, websites, code. From all of it, it learned one skill: given everything so far, which word most likely comes next. Ask it to write a polite email to a client who's paying late. It scores every possible first word ("Hi" 40%, "Dear" 35%, "Hey" 5%), picks one, adds it, and does it again. About two hundred times for one short email. That's the whole engine. It also explains AI hallucinations. It writes what sounds right. When it doesn't know, it doesn't stop, so you get confident, smooth and wrong. The fix: give it your real documents and ask where the answer came from. AI images and video work on the same idea. Most models start from pure static, like an old TV, and sculpt the noise toward your words step by step. Step 1 static, step 10 blurry shapes, step 30 a mug, step 50 light catching the rim. The picture on the TV in this video is a real run, all 50 steps saved and played back. Three rules for getting better results from AI: It predicts from what's in front of it, so give it context. Vague words get average results, so describe exactly what you want. It sounds sure even when it's wrong, so check the facts that matter. The AI agent reads the row and your brand guide, writes the real prompt, and picks the format: vertical video for TikTok, square image for the store. 4. The 4 levels of AI agents There are four levels of AI agents, and most people call level one an agent. Chatbot. Underneath, it's a model that predicts words. It can't touch anything outside the chat window. Ask it to reschedule a client and it tells you how. You still do the work. The test: if it can't change anything in your apps, it's a chatbot, whatever the label says. Assistant. What changes is tools: a connection into one app, with a list of things the AI is allowed to do there. Read the calendar, move an event, send an email. Ask it to move a client to Thursday and it does it in thirty seconds instead of five minutes. But it's one request, one action, and it waits for you every time. Agent. Stop giving it steps and give it a goal: get every overdue client paid this week. It runs a loop (plan, act, check): reads the invoices, sends a reminder, checks back, sends a softer one, updates the books when they pay, and stops. An intern gets tasks. A manager gets a target. And it only gets the tools that job needs. It can read invoices. It can't issue refunds. AI employee. Same agent, but it doesn't wait for you at all. It has a job description, a memory of every client, and a schedule. Every morning at eight it checks who's overdue, chases them and updates the books. Anything risky, like a refund, waits for your approval. You stop asking. You approve. #aiagents #aiemployee #aiautomation

AI answers correctly when your business is written down in a structure it can look up. How to build an AI email assistant for your business: Map your inbox. Connect Gmail, pull the last 3 months of customer emails, and let AI sort them into the types you really get: prices, reschedules, complaints, access, special requests. For each type, write down how you handle it. That one page is your playbook, and it's the base of every AI customer service system. Put your clients in one Google Sheet. One row per client, matched by email and phone number, with a column for each home's rules ("dog stays inside", "no bleach"). Lockbox codes and passwords never go in a sheet the AI reads. Write one doc of general business rules: prices, hours, what you don't do. The AI workflow: a new email comes in, AI sorts it, matches the sender to their row, reads the rules and drafts a reply from that data. Add a checker. A second AI step checks every draft against the sheet and the rules: right day, right price, nothing made up. If it fails, the email goes to you. Human in the loop. Easy emails, like a starting price, can send on their own. Complaints, refunds, schedule changes, access and unknown senders go to you as a Gmail draft or a Slack message, so you approve before anything goes out. Roll it out safely. Test it on your old emails first, run 2 weeks of drafts only, and turn on automation one email type at a time. Let it learn. When you edit a draft, the AI suggests a new rule and you approve it, so the system gets better without rewriting itself. Add text messages.
